paras: The St. Louis Workhouse quarry bombing was an explosion on June 12, 1919, in the rock quarry of the City Workhouse in St. Louis, Missouri, in which a white prisoner threw an explosive among Black prisoners, injuring eleven to thirteen of them. St. Louis daily papers reported the episode as a "race riot" in which guards fired on fighting prisoners, a version that also reached the Wisconsin Weekly Blade. The St. Louis Argus, a Black weekly, investigated and called those reports "false and misleading", describing instead one man's act followed by an attempted mass escape by white prisoners.

The City Workhouse stood at 4200 South Broadway, and its prisoners, white and Black, worked together in a rock quarry under Superintendent H. N. Morgan. According to the Argus, there had been "some ill feeling on the part of the whites against the Negroes," and white prisoners complained that Morgan was "partial to the Colored men" and granted them more favors. Director of Public Welfare Schmoll told the paper that the workhouse was being filled with "hardened criminals" who had pleaded guilty to lesser sentences to avoid the penitentiary.

At about four o'clock on the afternoon of Thursday, June 12, a white prisoner threw an explosive near or into a group of Black prisoners working in the quarry. The morning paper quoted by the Argus described a bottle of nitroglycerin followed by "two other deafening explosions," while the Argus described a single dynamite bomb "of the tomato can variety" that wounded thirteen Black prisoners, none seriously.

What followed is told differently in the two versions. In the daily-paper account, 165 prisoners, 75 of them white, fought with picks, sledgehammers and rocks, and sixteen armed guards led by Morgan fired on them, shooting six Black prisoners and one white prisoner. In the Argus account, the bomb was the signal for about 75 white prisoners to break for escape, and a guard fired a single shot into them that struck one man in the shoulder; the paper's text also reads that "the other was killed," a phrase it does not explain.

Workhouse officials, according to the Argus, found homemade dynamite bombs "planted" in several places and concluded that prisoners had planned to blow up the workhouse and escape in the confusion. Several prisoners were transferred to the City Jail the following Tuesday to serve out their sentences, and the Argus headline reported "Plotters Sent To Jail." No report of criminal charges or a trial for the bombing was found in the coverage.

The St. Louis dailies framed the episode as a "race riot," and the Argus reprinted a long passage from one morning paper describing a "battle" between "two fighting parties" of prisoners. On June 20 the Argus answered on its front page under the headline "Prisoners Planned Get-Away" and the heading "The Truth About the Troubles," stating flatly that "there was no riot" and that the bombing was "purely a personal matter." The paper stressed that "no Negro was injured" by gunfire and that there was "no fighting between the white and Colored," shifting the story from racial conflict to a white escape plot.

The riot version nonetheless travelled in the Black press: on June 26 the Wisconsin Weekly Blade carried a one-paragraph St. Louis item reporting one white man and twelve Black prisoners injured, "several seriously," and police reserves called when guards could not quell the "rioters."

The accounts disagree on whether a riot took place, on who was shot, and on the number and seriousness of injuries: eleven Black prisoners in the morning paper, twelve in the Blade, and thirteen, none seriously, in the Argus. The Argus version rests on its own reporter's inquiry and on workhouse officials, while the riot version comes from a quoted daily and an unattributed brief.

reader.title: St. Louis Workhouse quarry bombing
bases: Both versions agree the violence began when a white prisoner threw an explosive (dynamite bomb or nitroglycerin bottle) at or near Black prisoners in the workhouse quarry (A1, A3); the daily-paper version calls the ensuing events a race riot (A1, A5), which the Argus denies (A2, A3).

The St. Louis Argus investigated and called the daily-paper 'race riot' reports 'false and misleading', denying any fighting between white and Black prisoners and any shooting of Black prisoners (A1, A2, A3), while the quoted morning paper and the Wisconsin Weekly Blade describe a riot (A1, A5); all accounts agree a white prisoner's explosive injured Black prisoners.

accounts.label: St. Louis morning paper (quoted by the Argus)
accounts.gist: A race riot among 165 prisoners began when a white prisoner threw a bottle of nitroglycerin near Black workers; guards fired on the fighters, shooting six Black men and a white man, and five other Black men and a Mexican were cut and bruised.

accounts.label: Argus reporter
accounts.gist: There was no riot: one white man threw a dynamite bomb into a crowd of Black prisoners, wounding thirteen slightly; about 75 white prisoners then tried to escape and a guard fired one shot at them, hitting no Black prisoner.

accounts.label: Workhouse officials (via the Argus)
accounts.gist: Prisoners had planned a wholesale escape, with homemade dynamite bombs 'planted' in several places to blow up the place.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: One white man and twelve Black prisoners were injured in a race riot in the quarry that sixteen guards could not quell, and police reserves were called.

framing.detail: The St. Louis Argus called the daily papers' 'Race Riot' reports 'false and misleading', ran 'The Truth About the Troubles', and recast the event as a white prisoner's personal act and an escape plot (front page).
The Wisconsin Weekly Blade ran a one-paragraph 'ST LOUS' brief repeating the 'race riot' version without comment.

quotes: Daily newspaper reports of a "Race Riot" at the City Workhouse, Thursday, June 12, were found, upon investigation, by an Argus reporter, to be false and misleading.
The riot started when one of the white men threw a bottle containing nitrolycerin near where the Negroes were working.

quotes: There was no riot. The Negroes and the whites work together and get along generally very well.
This was purely a personal matter and did not involve the mass of prisoners.
